title: Characterization Method Finder: pick an instrument for your sample
description: Filter characterization and testing methods (SEM, EDS, TEM, XRD, XPS, SIMS, ICP, DSC, hardness, ultrasonic testing and more) by what you need to know and what your sample allows, then compare resolution, detection limit, preparation and pitfalls side by side.
lead: This page helps you decide which instrument to use when you have a sample and a question. Choose what you want to know and the constraints of your sample; suitable methods are listed in order, and methods that do not fit are set aside with the reason. Pick two to four methods to compare side by side, including preparation before measuring and pitfalls in reading the results.
note: Values are typical values from the sources and vary greatly with instrument, conditions and material. Use them as a guide for comparing methods and narrowing down candidates, and check with the instrument manager or service lab before measuring. Standards are listed by name, number and scope only (see the standards themselves for specimen dimensions and conditions).

needs.decomp: Decomposition, moisture and filler content (mass change on heating)

guide.h: How to think about resolution, detection limit and analyzed volume
p: Method numbers differ by orders of magnitude because what you probe with and what you collect fixes the size of the region the signal comes from. SEM secondary electrons escape only from the top ~15 nm, so images are sharp, while X-rays from the same beam (EDS) come from the whole 1–few µm interaction volume, so composition maps are µm-scale. XPS and AES see a few nm, XRD a few to tens of µm, and neutrons several cm into steel.

The detection limit is set by the ratio of signal to background. EDS peaks are broad (tens of eV up to about 250 eV) and sit on the continuum, so about 0.1 wt% is the limit; WDS separates wavelengths with a crystal, giving narrow peaks (a few to tens of eV) and limits around 100 ppm. ICP-MS, which dissolves the sample and counts ions one by one, reaches ppb levels in the solid.

Resolution and detection limit tend to trade off. A smaller volume contains fewer atoms, so minor elements become harder to see: APT gives about 10 ppm at 0.3 nm resolution, TEM-EDS about 0.5 wt% at a nm spot, and ICP reaches ppb by giving up spatial information. Decide both where and down to what level you need to know before choosing.

The values in the tables are typical values from the sources. They vary a lot with instrument generation, conditions and material, so ask the instrument manager or service lab for the value on your sample.

guide.h: Qualitative versus quantitative, and which analyzes need standards
p: "What is there" (qualitative) and "how much" (quantitative) are different questions. EDS spot analysis is qualitative within seconds, but it becomes quantitative to a few percent relative for major elements only on a flat polished sample compared against standards of known composition. Treat standardless results as semi-quantitative, not as quantitative values for a paper.

Standards are essentially required for WDS (EPMA), SIMS (ion-implanted standards), XRF (similar-composition standards), ICP (solution calibration), combustion and fusion analysis (certified reference materials) and GD-OES. XPS and AES are mostly semi-quantitative with sensitivity factors, and XRD has difficulty seeing phases below about 1%.

Standards should have a similar matrix, because the signal from the same amount of an element changes with absorption and excitation by the surrounding elements (matrix effects). When outsourcing, ask for the standards used for calibration together with the results.

Write the aim in one sentence. If it is "find why hardness dropped after heat treatment", what you need is the change in microstructure (optical microscopy, SEM), the precipitates (TEM) and the hardness profile (hardness testing), perhaps not precise composition.
Decide what to compare with. Measuring only the failed part shows no difference without a good part. Measure good, failed and untreated samples side by side with the same method and conditions.

Decide numbers and statistics: how many hardness indents, how many fields for grain size, how many fatigue specimens, and report the scatter (standard deviation). One microscope field or one APT needle may not represent the whole sample.
Assume that preparation changes the result. Record preparation and storage: polishing scratches, FIB damage, coatings, grinding stresses, hydrogen loss during storage and so on.

guide.h: What to tell a service lab
p: What you want to know (the aim) and what decision the result will feed. Giving the aim, not just a method name, lets the lab suggest a better method or conditions.

About the sample: material type and expected composition, heat-treatment and processing history, size and number, conductivity, magnetism, whether it may go into vacuum, presence of moisture, oil or organics, and whether it contains toxic or radioactive substances.
Where to measure: which face, depth or region (mark it on a photo), and whether to compare with a good part.

The form of the result: required detection limit, resolution and precision, candidate elements or phases, a statement of standards and calibration, whether raw data are needed, deadline and budget. Say in advance whether the sample must come back (destructive or not).

faq: Can I report C or O amounts from EDS?

Light elements such as C, N and O are strongly absorbed and their peaks change shape between compounds, so EDS quantification can be far off. C cannot be measured on carbon-coated samples, and O is often calculated. Use EDS only as a guide to presence; measure amounts with WDS (with standards) or, for C in steel, combustion analysis.
Why does XRD crystallite size differ from the grain size I see in the microscope?

The Scherrer crystallite size is the average size of coherently diffracting domains, and one particle or grain may contain many of them. Above about 100 nm the estimate is unreliable, and strain broadening also mixes in. Measure grain size with optical microscopy, SEM or EBSD.
Are bright areas in a BSE image heavy elements?

On a flat polished surface BSE brightness is set mainly by mean atomic number, so bright areas tend to be heavier on average. But topography and crystal orientation (channeling) also change brightness, so on fracture surfaces or poorly polished samples confirm with EDS rather than reading contrast as composition.
For internal flaws without cutting, how do I choose between UT, radiography and CT?

UT suits thick parts and structures on site and gives flaw depth, but needs couplant and skill and struggles with coarse grains. Radiography leaves a record and is strong on volumetric flaws such as porosity, but cracks may not show depending on orientation and depth is unknown. CT gives 3-D shape and position, but resolution falls as samples get larger and the sample must fit the instrument.
Do the values in the tables apply to my instrument?

They are typical values from the sources and vary a lot with instrument generation, conditions and sample. Use them to compare methods and narrow down candidates, and check the values for your sample with the instrument manager or service lab before measuring.

om.name: Optical (metallurgical) microscopy
om.what: Look at a polished and etched section to see grain size, phase distribution, inclusions and layer thickness. The first step in examining a microstructure.
om.how: Metals are viewed in reflected light. An etchant attacks grain boundaries and phases at different rates, which turns them into light and dark contrast.
om.rl: About 0.2 µm (limit set by the wavelength of light)
om.rd: Image of the polished plane (no depth information)
om.el: None (phases are inferred from color, shape and etching response)
om.q: Area fractions and grain size can be quantified by image analysis
om.size: Powders and small pieces can be mounted in resin; large parts must be sectioned
om.ds: The sectioned and polished part is destroyed
om.prep: Cut → mount in resin → polish → etch. Half a day to a day, depending on material and etchant
om.time: Minutes to tens of minutes once the sample is ready
om.cost: Usually cheap on a shared university instrument
miss: Polishing scratches and smeared layers are highlighted by etching and can be mistaken for microstructure. Etching does not remove earlier damage
Resolution is about 0.2 µm, so fine precipitates and the inside of martensite laths are not resolved (go to SEM or TEM)
A section is a 2-D cut, so grain shape and size look different depending on the cutting direction. For rolled material, examine several sections in defined directions
std: ASTM E3 (guide to preparing metallographic specimens)
ASTM E407 (microetching metals and alloys)
JIS G 0551 / ASTM E112 (determining grain size)
ISO 3887 (determining the depth of decarburization of steels)

sem.name: Scanning electron microscopy (SE and BSE imaging)
sem.what: Image surface topography (SE) and differences in mean atomic number (BSE) with far better resolution and depth of field than an optical microscope. The workhorse for fracture surfaces and fine microstructure.
sem.how: A finely focused electron beam is scanned over the surface, and the number of secondary electrons (SE) and backscattered electrons (BSE) coming out sets the brightness of each pixel.
sem.rl: About 1–5 nm (around 1 nm with a field-emission gun, about 5 nm on a typical instrument)
sem.rd: SE from the top ~15 nm; BSE from deeper (depends on accelerating voltage)
sem.vol: SE: the very surface; BSE: the upper part of the electron interaction volume
sem.el: Not from the image (BSE brightness is only a guide to mean atomic number)
sem.q: Calibrate the magnification with a standard before measuring sizes
sem.size: Whatever fits the chamber (instrument dependent); large parts must be cut
sem.cond: Insulators need a ~10 nm conductive coating or low-vacuum imaging
sem.vac: Normally high vacuum; wet samples must be dried or imaged in low vacuum
sem.ds: Non-destructive for surfaces; sections must be cut and polished
sem.prep: Little for surfaces; polishing for sections; coating for insulators
sem.time: Tens of minutes to a few hours per sample
sem.cost: Usually cheap on a shared university instrument
miss: Reading BSE contrast as composition. Topography and crystal orientation (channeling) also change the brightness, so check on a flat polished surface together with EDS
Mistaking charging artifacts (bright, smeared areas) on insulators, or the grain of a coating, for microstructure
Trusting the on-screen scale as is. Calibrate the magnification with a standard before measuring sizes

ebsd.name: Electron backscatter diffraction
ebsd.what: Map the orientation of every grain to obtain grain size, texture, grain-boundary misorientation, phase distribution (by crystal structure) and a guide to local strain.
ebsd.how: In the SEM the sample is tilted to 70°, the diffraction pattern of backscattered electrons (Kikuchi pattern) is recorded, and the crystal orientation is solved point by point.
ebsd.rl: 20–80 nm (material dependent). Grains smaller than 50 nm are difficult (TKD on a thin foil reaches 2–20 nm)
ebsd.el: None (combine with simultaneous EDS to separate phases)
ebsd.q: Orientation precision about 0.2° (about 0.001° with cross-correlation analysis for strain)
ebsd.cond: A conductive coating weakens the patterns, so low-vacuum imaging is preferred for insulators
ebsd.ds: Needs a flat polished surface, so that part is cut and polished
ebsd.prep: Mechanical polishing followed by a strain-free finish (chemical or electrolytic polishing). Laborious
ebsd.time: Tens of minutes to hours per map (fast detectors exceed 3000 points per second)
miss: Polishing damage left at the surface kills the patterns and leaves many points unindexed. Mechanical polishing alone is often not enough
Grain size depends on the misorientation threshold used to define a boundary and on the step size. State them when comparing
The mapped area is small (hundreds of µm to mm). Check the texture of the whole sheet with XRD pole figures

tem.name: Transmission electron microscopy (BF, DF, HRTEM, STEM-HAADF)
tem.what: Image dislocations, precipitates and interfaces down to atomic columns using electrons transmitted through a specimen thinner than 100 nm. With electron diffraction and EDS/EELS, structure and composition come from the same spot.
tem.how: Bright- and dark-field contrast comes from differences in diffracted intensity, and HRTEM forms lattice images by interference of transmitted and diffracted waves. STEM-HAADF collects electrons scattered to high angles, so heavier atoms look brighter (Z contrast).
tem.rl: 0.1–0.3 nm (TEM point resolution 0.14 nm, 0.1 nm in an aberration-corrected STEM; about 0.2–0.25 nm without correction)
tem.rd: Projection through the whole specimen thickness (<100 nm)
tem.dl: EDS about 0.5 wt% (0.01–0.1 wt% under good conditions)
tem.vol: A region of µm size or less in a foil thinner than 100 nm
tem.el: EDS from B upwards (poor sensitivity to light elements); EELS down to Li
tem.q: EDS is semi-quantitative to a few percent
tem.size: Disks about 3 mm across, particles on a grid, or FIB lamellae
tem.ds: Destroys the part that is thinned
tem.prep: Thin by electropolishing, ion milling, FIB or ultramicrotomy. Needs skill and time
miss: The volume examined is tiny (<100 nm thick, µm across). One field may not represent the sample, so survey with SEM first and then choose the site
Preparation damage mistaken for microstructure. FIB lamellae carry a Ga-damaged layer on both faces; milling at 30 kV alone leaves about 20 nm per side in Si
Bright- and dark-field contrast mainly reflects diffraction. Check whether it is compositional with HAADF (brightness set by atomic number) or EDS

fib.name: Focused ion beam
fib.what: Mill a chosen site with µm precision to expose a cross-section or to make TEM lamellae and APT needles. Combined with an SEM, repeated slice-and-image gives 3-D microstructure.
fib.how: Ga ions focused below 10 nm sputter atoms from the surface. The milled face is imaged with the electron beam (SEM).
fib.rl: Beam below 10 nm; imaging at SEM resolution (about 1 nm)
fib.rd: Serial sectioning gives 3-D data on regions 100 nm–10 µm in size
fib.vol: A local region of µm to tens of µm
fib.cond: Insulators charge and should be coated
fib.prep: Decide the site first; deposit a protective layer before milling
fib.time: Hours per cross-section; half a day to a day per TEM lamella
fib.cost: Medium to high (instrument time is expensive)
miss: The milled face carries a Ga-damaged layer (about 20 nm per side in Si at 30 kV). Finish TEM lamellae at low voltage (3–7 nm at 2 kV)
The accessible area is small, so locate the feature with SEM or optical microscopy before milling

afm.name: Atomic force microscopy
afm.what: Trace the surface with a sharp tip and build a height map at nm scale. Measures roughness, steps and particle heights without vacuum, on insulators too.
afm.how: A laser reads the deflection of the cantilever carrying the tip, and the height is followed so that the tip–surface force stays constant.
afm.vol: Surface only (scan up to about 90 µm square and 5 µm in height)
afm.q: Height values depend on tip shape and scan conditions
afm.size: Small pieces to wafers (some stages take 300 mm)
afm.time: Minutes to tens of minutes per site
afm.cost: Usually cheap on a shared university instrument
miss: The tip shape is convolved into the image: a blunt tip makes narrow trenches look shallower and narrower and bumps look wider
The field of view is small (up to about 90 µm). Survey with an optical microscope and pick a representative site
Steps above a few µm and very rough surfaces are a problem (use a laser confocal microscope or white-light interferometer)

optprof.name: Laser confocal microscopy and white-light interferometry
optprof.what: Measure the 3-D shape of a surface optically and without contact, and turn roughness, steps, wear-scar depth and indent shape into numbers.
optprof.how: A laser confocal microscope picks up only in-focus light to find the height; a white-light interferometer finds the height where the interference fringes are strongest.
optprof.rl: About 0.3–0.5 µm (lateral resolution is diffraction-limited, 0.61λ/NA: about 0.26 µm at 405 nm and NA 0.95; 0.5 µm in a white-light interferometer example)
optprof.rd: White-light interferometry 0.1 nm (phase mode) to 6 nm (scanning mode)
optprof.vol: Surface only (one field is mm-sized, stitched up to several cm)
optprof.q: Data drop out or go wrong on steep slopes and under transparent films
optprof.size: Small pieces to parts tens of cm across (depends on the stage)
optprof.cost: Usually cheap on a shared university instrument
miss: On steep or rough surfaces light does not return, leaving gaps or noise in the data
Under a transparent film, light returns from both the film surface and the interface, distorting the shape. Film thickness can be measured only for transparent films of known refractive index
Roughness values depend on the evaluation length or area and on the filter (cut-off). Use the same conditions when comparing

stylus.name: Stylus profilometer (roughness and step height)
stylus.what: Trace the surface with a diamond stylus to measure step heights (film thickness) and surface roughness, over long distances in one scan (up to 150 mm on one instrument).
stylus.how: A stylus pressed on with a small force is moved across the surface, and its vertical motion is recorded as a surface profile.
stylus.rl: Set by the stylus tip radius (2 µm for a standard stylus)
stylus.rd: Heights down to the ångström level (instrument example)
stylus.q: Valleys narrower than the stylus and steep slopes are rounded off by the stylus shape
stylus.size: Small pieces to plates on the stage; portable units measure on large parts (scan lengths up to 150 mm on one instrument)
stylus.ds: The stylus touches the surface (the force can be set low)
stylus.prep: Almost none (film thickness is measured at a step)
miss: Features finer than the stylus tip (for example 2 µm) are not resolved; valleys come out shallow and peaks broad
Only one line is measured, so check variation by measuring several lines
Film thickness is measured as a step, so part of the film has to be removed to make one

xrr.name: X-ray reflectometry
xrr.what: Shine X-rays at grazing angles on a thin film on a flat substrate and use the change of reflectivity with angle to obtain film thickness, density and interface width (roughness). For single and multilayer films about 1 nm to 1 µm thick.
xrr.how: Reflectivity is measured from near the critical angle of total reflection upward, and thickness, density and interface width are found by fitting a curve calculated from a layer model.
xrr.rl: — (average over the X-ray footprint, which must be laterally uniform)
xrr.rd: Films about 1 nm to 1 µm thick
xrr.el: Elements are not measured directly (no chemical information)
xrr.q: A layer model (number and order of layers) is assumed for fitting, so a different model gives different values
xrr.ds: Non-destructive (the film must not change during the measurement)
xrr.time: Measurement and model fitting take time
miss: A substrate that is not flat, or a film that is laterally non-uniform within the footprint, cannot be analyzed
Surface contamination or reacted layers act as extra layers. Keep the surface clean before measuring
XRR alone gives no elements or chemical states. Combine with XPS or similar for composition
std: ISO 16413 (thickness, density and interface width of thin films by X-ray reflectometry)

ellips.name: Spectroscopic ellipsometry
ellips.what: Measure the change in polarization of reflected light (Ψ and Δ) at many wavelengths to obtain thin-film thickness and optical constants such as refractive index, without contact or damage. Sensitive to sub-monolayer changes, and up to tens of µm for transparent films.
ellips.how: Polarized light is reflected at an oblique angle and the change in polarization is measured. The data do not give thickness directly; a layer model with optical-constant dispersion formulas is fitted to them.
ellips.rd: Sensitive to sub-monolayer changes; about 0.5 nm to 20 µm for transparent films (instrument example)
ellips.el: Elements are not measured (optical constants are)
ellips.q: A layer model and dispersion formulas are assumed for fitting, so a different model gives different values
ellips.size: Flat, reflective samples (wafers, glass plates, etc.)
ellips.cond: Not needed (dielectric, organic, semiconductor and metal films)
ellips.time: Each point is quick, but model fitting can take time
miss: Thickness comes from fitting a model to Ψ and Δ, so wrong assumptions about the layers or optical constants give wrong values
Surfaces that are not flat or do not reflect light cannot be measured
Compare with XRR or cross-sections to check that the model is reasonable

xct.name: X-ray computed tomography
xct.what: Record X-ray radiographs while rotating the sample to see internal pores, cracks, inclusions and fiber orientation in 3-D without cutting.
xct.how: The X-ray attenuation at each point (set by density and atomic number) is reconstructed by computation from projections taken in many directions.
xct.rl: About 1/1000–1/2000 of the sample width (finer for smaller samples: µm for mm-sized samples; instruments reaching 0.1 µm exist)
xct.dl: — (small density differences are hard to see)
xct.vol: The whole sample (mm to tens of cm, as far as X-rays penetrate)
xct.q: Porosity and defect volume depend on how the image threshold is set
xct.size: From a pellet of powder to large parts (resolution drops as size grows)
xct.time: Hours to a day for scanning and reconstruction
miss: Resolution is set by sample size. A large part scanned whole will not show fine cracks; cut out a smaller piece if needed
Artifacts such as beam hardening (bright rim, dark center) mistaken for density differences
Closed cracks and phases of similar density are hard to distinguish

eds.name: Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
eds.what: Find out quickly which elements are present, and roughly how much, at a point, line or area hit by the electron beam in an SEM or TEM. Good for element maps.
eds.how: The beam knocks out inner-shell electrons, and a semiconductor detector sorts and counts the characteristic X-rays by energy.
eds.rl: 1 to a few µm in the SEM (set by the interaction volume); a few nm in a thin TEM foil
eds.rd: 1 to a few µm in the SEM
eds.dl: 0.1–0.5 wt% (0.02–0.05 wt% reported under good conditions)
eds.el: Be–U (Be–F can be detected but are hard to quantify; H, He and Li cannot be measured)
eds.q: A few percent relative for major elements on a flat polished surface against standards; standardless results carry larger errors and are semi-quantitative
eds.cond: Insulators need a carbon (or other) coating or low vacuum (semi-quantitative in low vacuum)
eds.ds: Surfaces can be measured as they are (quantification needs a polished surface; depth or layer thickness needs a cut section)
eds.prep: Almost none for qualitative work; a flat polished surface for quantification
eds.time: Seconds to minutes per point; tens of minutes to hours per map
eds.cost: Cheap; usually fitted to the SEM
miss: Trusting quantified C, N and O. Light-element X-rays are strongly absorbed and their peaks change shape between compounds. C cannot be measured on carbon-coated samples, and O is often calculated rather than measured
Peak overlaps (S, Mo and Pb near 2.3 keV; Ti and Ba; Ti and V) lead to reporting elements that are not there
Spot analysis of particles or layers smaller than 1–2 µm also picks up the surroundings and the substrate
Rough fracture surfaces and loose powders do not give correct quantitative values (quantify on flat polished surfaces)
std: ISO 22309 (quantitative EDS analysis of elements from Na upwards)

wds.name: Wavelength-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EPMA)
wds.what: With about ten times the spectral resolution of EDS, quantify trace elements down to ~100 ppm and elements with overlapping peaks accurately against standards. Also used for line scans such as carbon profiles across case-hardened layers.
wds.how: Characteristic X-rays are Bragg-reflected by an analyzing crystal and counted wavelength by wavelength; each spectrometer measures one wavelength at a time.
wds.rl: 1 to a few µm (set by the interaction volume)
wds.dl: 100–300 ppm (a few ppm under favourable conditions)
wds.el: Be (B on some instruments) to U. H, He and Li cannot be measured; errors grow for Be–O
wds.q: 0.5–1.5% relative for major elements (>1 wt%); standards are essential
wds.size: Flat samples from a few hundred µm to about 50 mm (one facility's example)
wds.prep: Polish to a flat mirror finish and carbon coat
wds.time: Minutes per point; longer with many elements
miss: Without standards there is no accuracy. Calibrate with standards of similar composition
Oxidation states such as Fe²⁺ versus Fe³⁺ cannot be distinguished
Spectrometers scan one wavelength at a time, so many elements take long. Screen the elements with EDS first
std: ISO 3887 (determining the depth of decarburization of steels)

xrf.name: X-ray fluorescence
xrf.what: Determine elements from Na to U nondestructively and quickly from the fluorescent X-rays excited by an X-ray beam. Used for alloy sorting, plating composition and thickness, and powders or liquids.
xrf.how: Primary X-rays eject inner-shell electrons, and the element-specific fluorescent X-rays emitted as the atoms relax are sorted by energy (ED) or wavelength (WD).
xrf.rl: Usually an average over a mm-sized area (tens of µm with micro-XRF)
xrf.rd: A few µm to several mm (strongly dependent on the X-ray line and the matrix)
xrf.dl: Around ppm (instrument and element dependent; worse for light elements)
xrf.el: Usually Na–U. WDXRF with multilayer analyzers also reaches Be–O (including C, N and O), but sensitivity and accuracy drop for elements lighter than Na (H and Li cannot be measured; handheld units cannot measure elements lighter than Mg)
xrf.q: Accurate when calibrated with standards of similar composition; standardless fundamental-parameter results are convenient but can carry large errors in some matrices
xrf.size: Powders and liquids to large parts (large parts with a handheld unit on site)
xrf.vac: Not needed (vacuum or helium improves light-element sensitivity)
xrf.prep: Measured as is; fused beads or pressed pellets for better accuracy
miss: Reading the composition of plating, oxide, paint or dirt as that of the base metal. The information depth ranges from a few µm to several mm depending on the element
Matrix effects change the intensities, so values are off unless calibrated with standards of similar composition
Light elements (lighter than Na) lose sensitivity and accuracy even with WDXRF and are not measured by ED or handheld units. Use combustion analysis for C in steel
std: ISO 3497 (coating thickness by X-ray spectrometry)

icp.name: ICP optical emission and ICP mass spectrometry
icp.what: Dissolve the sample in acid and feed the solution into a hot plasma to quantify about 70 elements: down to ppm in the solid with ICP-OES and ppb with ICP-MS. The standard route to average composition and trace impurities.
icp.how: A hot argon plasma excites and ionizes the atoms; elements are sorted by emission wavelength (OES) or ion mass (MS).
icp.dl: About 1 ppm in the solid for ICP-OES and 10 ppb for ICP-MS (solution limits multiplied by the dissolution and dilution factor; interferences make them an order of magnitude worse or more)
icp.vol: All the dissolved material (one facility asks for at least 1 g of solid)
icp.el: About 70 elements. ICP-OES cannot measure C, N, O, halogens, noble gases or H (one facility's list)
icp.q: Uncertainty of 5% or less (20% or less near the limit) in one facility's example
icp.size: Powder, chips or small pieces (cut from large parts)
icp.prep: Dissolve completely in acid (HF or fusion for refractory materials). Laborious
icp.time: Hours to a day to dissolve; weeks to a month if outsourced
miss: Losing elements through undissolved residue or volatilization. Complete dissolution is assumed
Spectral overlaps (OES) and polyatomic ions (MS) produce false or inflated results
Taking the solution detection limit as the limit in the solid (multiply by the dilution factor)
No information on spatial distribution (segregation, surface layers)

gas.name: Combustion and inert gas fusion analysis (C, S, O, N, H)
gas.what: Quantify C and S (combustion) and O, N and H (inert gas fusion) in metals quickly, down to ppm levels. Used for carbon in steel, oxygen and hydrogen in titanium, hydrogen in weld metal and so on.
gas.how: Combustion burns the sample in oxygen and measures the CO₂ and SO₂ by infrared absorption. Inert gas fusion melts the sample in a graphite crucible and measures the CO (from O), N₂ and H₂ by infrared absorption or thermal conductivity.
gas.dl: From about 0.1 ppm (element and instrument dependent)
gas.vol: The whole sample burned or fused
gas.el: C, S, O, N and H only
gas.size: Chips or small pieces (cut from large parts)
gas.prep: Cut to a set size and remove surface contamination
gas.cost: Medium (fewer instruments, but analysis is fast)
miss: Diffusible hydrogen escapes quickly even at room temperature. In weld metal the value falls the longer the delay (about 20% between 20 s and 300 s before quenching in liquid nitrogen in one study), so keep samples cold
Total hydrogen (fusion) and diffusible hydrogen released on heating are different quantities. State which was measured
No spatial information (segregation, decarburized or carburized layers). Use EPMA, GD-OES or hardness profiles on a section
std: ASTM E1019 (C, S, N and O in steel, iron, Ni and Co alloys)
ASTM E1447 (H in reactive metals such as Ti and Zr)
ISO 3690 (diffusible hydrogen in weld metal)

spark.name: Spark optical emission spectrometry
spark.what: Fire a spark between a metal sample and an electrode and use the emitted light to determine many elements at once, including C, N, P, S and B. Used for composition control of steels, cast irons and nonferrous metals.
spark.how: A spark discharge in argon vaporizes and excites the sample surface, and the intensities of element-specific emission lines are measured. Lines of C, N, P and S lie in the vacuum ultraviolet, which air absorbs, so the spectrometer is evacuated.
spark.dl: Below 10 ppm for some elements (instrument examples: below 10 ppm for B and Pb, below 1 ppm for Zn)
spark.el: Many elements in metals, including C, N, P, S and B. N needs a capable instrument; use gas analysis for O and H (some instruments handle O in copper and H in titanium alloys)
spark.q: Calibrated with standards of similar composition (prepared the same way)
spark.size: Metal pieces that can be ground flat and cover the spark stand opening
spark.cond: Conductive metals only (the sample is an electrode)
spark.vac: Not needed (the sample is in argon; the spectrometer is evacuated)
spark.ds: Leaves a spark mark; the surface is ground
spark.prep: Grind the surface flat and keep it clean; spark on sound metal without pores or pits
miss: Sparking on pores or pits changes the discharge and gives wrong values. Grind and measure sound metal
Touching or contaminating the ground surface changes the result. Keep it clean after grinding
If standards are not prepared the same way as samples, the calibration does not match
std: ASTM E415 (spark atomic emission analysis of carbon and low-alloy steel)

gdoes.name: Glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy
gdoes.what: Sputter the surface with a glow discharge while recording the emitted light to obtain composition depth profiles from nm to about 100 µm (plating, nitrided layers, oxides, paint) for almost all elements including H, in a short time.
gdoes.how: An argon glow discharge with the sample as cathode sputters surface atoms; their emission in the plasma is dispersed and recorded element by element against time (= depth).
gdoes.rl: — (average over a circle a few mm across; no lateral mapping)
gdoes.rd: About 10% of the depth (for layers thicker than 10 nm)
gdoes.vol: Sputtered circle × depth (nm to about 100 µm; over 150 µm reported)
gdoes.el: Almost all elements including H, C, N and O
gdoes.q: Calibrated with standards (matrix-independent calibration is possible)
gdoes.size: Pieces or sheets with a flat area larger than 4 mm across
gdoes.vac: No high vacuum, but the sample face is exposed to low-pressure argon
gdoes.prep: None if there is a flat surface
miss: Depth resolution is about 10% of the depth, so deeper interfaces look broader. Do not mistake the interface width for a diffusion width
Laterally everything is averaged: islands, local precipitates or non-uniform layers are not seen (laterally uniform layers are assumed)
Converting time to depth needs the sputter rate (material dependent) and a measured crater depth
std: ISO 3887 (determining the depth of decarburization of steels)

tds.name: Thermal desorption spectroscopy (hydrogen)
tds.what: Heat the sample at a constant rate and measure the hydrogen released at each temperature. Used to find how much hydrogen a steel contains and where (in which traps) it is held.
tds.how: The sample is heated and the released hydrogen is measured, either with a mass spectrometer in vacuum (TDS) or carried by argon to a gas chromatograph (TDA). Changing the heating rate shifts the desorption peak temperatures, and the shift gives the binding energy of each trap.
tds.dl: About 1 wt ppm (about 50 atomic ppm) in steel with one instrument
tds.q: Hydrogen held in different ways is separated by the desorption curve (peaks) versus temperature
tds.vac: Depends on the setup (TDS in vacuum; gas-chromatograph TDA in a furnace with flowing argon)
tds.ds: Cut out; heating drives the hydrogen out
tds.prep: Keep hydrogen-charged samples in liquid nitrogen until measurement so the hydrogen stays in
miss: Water adsorbed on the surface also gives a hydrogen peak (a peak near 350 °C after about a minute in laboratory air was reported). Decide how samples are handled
Diffusible hydrogen escapes even at room temperature. Keep samples cold between charging and measurement
In thin cut samples, surface working and condition shift the peak temperatures (cutting reduced the measured hydrogen in one report)

xps.name: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
xps.what: Identify the elements within a few nm of the surface and their chemical state (metal or oxide, bonding partner). The standard tool for passive films, contamination and plating adhesion failures.
xps.how: The kinetic energy of photoelectrons ejected by X-rays gives their binding energy, which identifies the element and shifts slightly with chemical state (chemical shift).
xps.rl: 10 µm to 2 mm (instrument dependent; smallest analysis areas of about 30–100 µm reported)
xps.vol: Tens of µm to mm across × a few nm
xps.el: Li–U (H and He cannot be measured)
xps.q: Mostly semi-quantitative with sensitivity factors. In sputter depth profiles, sputtering can change the chemical state
xps.size: Small pieces that fit the instrument (some take wafers)
xps.ds: Non-destructive for surface analysis; depth profiling sputters
xps.prep: Almost none (do not touch or contaminate the surface)
miss: It sees only the top few nm, so adventitious carbon and native oxide from air are easily mistaken for the composition of the material
Ion sputtering during depth profiling changes chemical states (for example by reduction). Do not over-trust states deep in the profile
Elements below about 0.1 at% are not seen

aes.name: Auger electron spectroscopy
aes.what: Analyze the elements in the top few nm at a chosen spot with an electron beam focused to 10–20 nm. Used for tiny particles, grain-boundary segregation and depth profiles of thin films.
aes.how: Elements are identified by the energy of Auger electrons emitted by atoms excited by the beam. Auger electrons can escape only from the top few nm.
aes.rl: 10 nm and above (beam can be focused to 10–20 nm)
aes.rd: Top 3–10 nm; 2–20 nm in depth profiles
aes.vol: A ~10 nm spot × a few nm
aes.q: Semi-quantitative with sensitivity factors (better against samples of known composition)
aes.size: Small pieces that fit the instrument (some take 300 mm wafers)
aes.ds: Non-destructive for surface analysis; depth profiling sputters
miss: Insulators charge and are hard to analyze (use XPS for chemical states of insulating surfaces)
Little chemical-state information (use XPS if you need the state)
Elements below 0.1–1 at% are not seen

sims.name: Secondary ion mass spectrometry
sims.what: Sputter the surface with ions and mass-analyze the secondary ions to obtain depth profiles of dopants and impurities below ppm levels (10¹⁰–10¹⁶ atoms/cm³).
sims.how: A primary ion beam (O₂⁺, Cs⁺ etc.) erodes the sample and the ejected ions are counted isotope by isotope in a mass spectrometer.
sims.rl: Depth profiles over areas of 10 µm and above; about 1 µm in imaging
sims.vol: µm to hundreds of µm across × depth (a few Å to tens of µm)
sims.el: H–U including isotopes (adsorbed water and hydrocarbons give a hydrogen background, suppressed by ultra-high vacuum and cryogenic trapping)
sims.q: Concentrations require standards (for example ion-implanted samples)
sims.size: Small pieces that fit the instrument
sims.cond: Insulators charge up, so charge compensation with an electron beam is needed (instrument dependent)
miss: Without standards there are no concentrations. Calibrate with standards in the same matrix (ion-implanted samples etc.)
Destructive: the crater remains and the spot cannot be reused
No chemical bonding information (use XPS for bonding)

apt.name: Atom probe tomography
apt.what: Field-evaporate atoms one by one from a needle-shaped specimen and reconstruct in 3-D which atom was where. Used for the composition of nm-sized precipitates, clusters and grain-boundary segregation.
apt.how: A needle cooled to 25–80 K is held at high voltage, and voltage or laser pulses ionize surface atoms; time of flight gives the mass and the detector position gives the original location.
apt.rl: 0.5 nm lateral and 0.3 nm in depth in metals (about 1 nm in semiconductors and insulators)
apt.el: H–U (residual hydrogen in the analysis chamber gives a background, so deuterium is sometimes used to tell them apart)
apt.q: Accuracy drops for elements with overlapping mass peaks
apt.size: A needle with apex radius below 100 nm (made by FIB etc.)
apt.cond: Voltage pulsing for conductors, laser pulsing for semiconductors and insulators
apt.ds: The part made into a needle is destroyed
apt.prep: Needles made by FIB etc. (hours each). Needs skill
miss: The analyzed volume is tiny (50 nm square × a few hundred nm). Choose the site with TEM or SEM before making the needle
Needles can fracture in the high field before the run is finished (material dependent)
Position and composition accuracy degrade at interfaces and in complex geometries

xrd.name: X-ray diffraction (powder and thin film)
xrd.what: Identify crystalline phases and measure lattice parameters, crystallite size, strain and crystallinity on powders, plates and thin films as they are, in a short time.
xrd.how: The positions and intensities of the diffracted beams that satisfy the Bragg condition (2d sinθ = λ) are matched against database (ICDD) patterns.
xrd.rl: Usually an average over 0.1 to several mm (20–25 µm with micro-diffraction)
xrd.rd: The 1/e attenuation depth of Cu Kα X-rays is about 4 µm in iron, 70 µm in Al and 3 mm in polyethylene (calculated from NIST attenuation coefficients); a few nm at grazing incidence
xrd.vol: Irradiated area × X-ray penetration depth (varies greatly with material)
xrd.el: Elements are not measured directly (seen as crystalline phases)
xrd.q: Phase fractions are approximate (phases below about 1% are missed)
xrd.size: Sub-milligram powders to plates and parts that fit the stage
xrd.time: Minutes to an hour per sample
miss: Confusing Scherrer "crystallite size" with grain or particle size. One particle can contain many crystallites. Above about 100 nm the estimate is unreliable, and instrumental broadening must be corrected and strain broadening separated
Amorphous phases give no peaks and cannot be identified
Phases below about 1% are missed
Powder packing or rolling texture changes intensity ratios so that patterns do not match the database

xrdrs.name: Residual stress and texture by X-ray diffraction
xrdrs.what: Measure near-surface residual stress from the shift of a diffraction peak (lattice spacing) while tilting the sample, and texture (pole figures) from the diffracted intensity as the orientation is changed.
xrdrs.how: In the sin²ψ method the spacing d is measured at several tilts ψ; stress follows from the slope of d against sin²ψ and the elastic constants of the measured plane.
xrdrs.rl: Average over the irradiated area (0.1 to several mm)
xrdrs.rd: Average over a few to tens of µm from the surface (5–50 µm in most materials; Cr Kα is used for steel). Deeper levels are measured after removing layers by electropolishing
xrdrs.vol: Irradiated area × a few to tens of µm
xrdrs.q: Coarse grains mean few diffracting grains and poorer precision (10–100 µm grains are fine)
xrdrs.size: Pieces to parts that fit the stage (portable instruments for large structures)
xrdrs.ds: Non-destructive (layers are removed by electropolishing for depth profiles)
xrdrs.prep: Measure the as-received surface; do not grind or polish
xrdrs.time: Tens of minutes to hours per point
miss: Grinding, machining or wire brushing adds surface stress. Measure as received, and remove layers only by electropolishing or chemical attack
It gives the stress within a few to tens of µm of the surface, not in the interior (use neutron diffraction for the interior)
Texture or coarse grains make d versus sin²ψ non-linear; taking a slope regardless gives wrong values
Use the elastic constants of the measured plane (X-ray elastic constants), not bulk values
std: ASTM E2860 (residual stress by XRD in bearing steels)
ASTM E81 (preparing quantitative pole figures)

ed.name: Electron diffraction (SAED and CBED)
ed.what: Determine crystal structure, orientation and orientation relationships from a selected region of nm to a few hundred nm inside the TEM. Identifies the phase of a single precipitate.
ed.how: The diffraction pattern of electrons transmitted through the specimen is recorded. Selected-area diffraction (SAED) chooses the region with an aperture; convergent-beam diffraction (CBED) takes the pattern from a finely focused probe.
ed.rl: SAED about 250 nm (set by the aperture); CBED a few nm
ed.vol: A small region of a thin foil
ed.q: Lattice spacings are usually accurate to 1–3% (0.1% with careful calibration), poorer than XRD
ed.ds: Destroys the part made into a foil
miss: Spacings are good to about 1–3%. Use XRD for precise lattice parameters
Errors in camera length (which changes with specimen height) shift d. Calibrate with a standard
The selected region is small, so phase fractions of the whole sample are unknown

nd.name: Neutron diffraction
nd.what: Because neutrons penetrate deep into metals, map residual stress inside components and study crystal structures containing light elements such as H and Li, and magnetic structures.
nd.how: Neutrons are scattered by nuclei. Scattering strength does not follow atomic number, so light elements that X-rays barely see, and isotopes of the same element, can be distinguished.
nd.vol: Total path length up to about 60 mm in steel and 100 mm in Al
nd.el: Light elements (H) and isotopes are easy to distinguish
nd.q: Stress accuracy about 10 MPa in Al and 30 MPa in steel in one example
nd.ds: Non-destructive (a stress-free reference may be cut out)
nd.time: Months from beam-time proposal; days of measurement
miss: A stress-free reference (d₀) is required, and how it is prepared changes the result a lot
Only possible at large facilities (reactors, accelerators), with long lead times from proposal to measurement
The near-surface region (tens of µm) is hard to resolve with mm-sized gauge volumes (use XRD for the surface)
std: ISO 21432 (residual stress by neutron diffraction)

dsc.name: Differential scanning calorimetry and differential thermal analysis
dsc.what: Measure the temperatures and heats of melting, crystallization, glass transition, precipitation and phase transformations while heating or cooling at a constant rate. Used for glass transitions and crystallinity of polymers and transformation temperatures of alloys.
dsc.how: DTA records the temperature difference between sample and reference, DSC the difference in heat flow. After calibration, DSC peak areas give heats.
dsc.dl: DSC is more sensitive than DTA, so weak events such as glass transitions are easier to see
dsc.q: Quantitative heats with DSC; DTA suits high temperatures (above 800 °C) and mainly gives temperatures
dsc.size: Small pieces or powder that fit the pan (cut from larger items)
dsc.vac: Not needed (usually under flowing inert gas)
dsc.ds: A small piece is cut and altered by heating
dsc.prep: Cut a small piece and seal it in a pan
dsc.time: One to a few hours per run
miss: Transition temperatures shift with heating rate. Compare samples at the same rate, and go slower for accurate values
Decomposition or evaporation overlapping a transition spoils the heat (use only while the sample mass is constant)
Solid-state transformations in metals can release little heat and be missed (combine with dilatometry)

tga.name: Thermogravimetric analysis
tga.what: Record the change in sample mass on heating to find moisture and volatiles, decomposition temperatures, filler content and weight gain from oxidation.
tga.how: The sample sits on a balance in a furnace and its mass is logged in inert or oxidizing gas.
tga.dl: Mass changes below a microgram (instrument example; samples of about 1–150 mg)
tga.vol: The whole sample (up to about 1 g in one example)
tga.size: Small pieces or powder that fit the pan
tga.ds: A small piece is cut and altered by heating
tga.prep: Cut a small piece and place it in the pan
tga.time: One to a few hours per run
miss: It does not say what was lost. Identify evolved gases with TGA-MS or TGA-FTIR
Results depend on the atmosphere (inert or air); weight gain by oxidation and loss by decomposition can overlap

dil.name: Dilatometry
dil.what: Record the change in length while changing temperature to obtain the thermal expansion coefficient, transformation temperatures of steels (Ac₁, Ac₃, Ms etc.) and sintering shrinkage.
dil.how: The extension of a rod specimen is transmitted by a push rod to a displacement sensor outside the furnace. Phase transformations change the volume, so the curve bends.
dil.q: Transformation temperatures and fractions are fixed by combining the curve with metallography
dil.prep: Machine a rod of set shape
dil.time: A few hours per run (depends on the thermal cycle)
miss: Transformation temperatures change with heating and cooling rates (and differ between continuous cooling and isothermal holding). State the conditions when comparing
Do not identify phases from kinks in the curve alone. Confirm with metallography
Rolled and composite materials expand differently in different directions. Record the specimen orientation
std: ASTM E228 (linear thermal expansion with a push-rod dilatometer)
ASTM A1033 (phase transformations of hypoeutectoid carbon and low-alloy steels)

lfa.name: Laser flash analysis
lfa.what: Heat the front of a thin disk with a light pulse and obtain thermal diffusivity from how fast the rear face warms up; multiply by specific heat and density for thermal conductivity.
lfa.how: An infrared detector records the rear-face temperature rise, and diffusivity is calculated from the thickness and the time to reach a set fraction of the maximum rise.
lfa.q: Conductivity is diffusivity times specific heat and density, so it carries their errors too
lfa.size: Small pieces that can be machined into disks
lfa.prep: Machine a disk; usually spray with graphite
lfa.time: Minutes per temperature; hours for a temperature series
miss: Translucent polymers and glasses, and shiny metals, need a graphite coating to be measured correctly. Too much graphite lowers the value for highly conductive Cu and Al (4% with a ~5 µm layer in one example)
Homogeneous, isotropic, opaque samples are assumed. Analyze layered or anisotropic materials with their orientation and structure in mind
Conductivity = diffusivity × specific heat × density, so errors in specific heat and density go straight into it
std: ASTM E1461 (thermal diffusivity by the flash method)

dma.name: Dynamic mechanical analysis
dma.what: Apply a small oscillating deformation while changing temperature to measure storage modulus, loss modulus and tan δ. Detects the glass transition of polymers more sensitively than DSC.
dma.how: The phase lag between oscillating force and deformation separates the elastic (E′) and viscous (E″) components. Tg is taken as the onset of the E′ drop, the E″ peak or the tan δ peak.
dma.dl: — (transitions hard to see by DSC are often clearer)
dma.q: Tg depends on the definition (E′ onset < E″ peak < tan δ peak) and on frequency. Use the same definition and frequency when comparing
dma.prep: Cut flat, untwisted bars or strips
miss: Tg differs between definitions (E′ onset, E″ peak, tan δ peak). State which was used
Higher frequencies give higher Tg. Compare at the same frequency
Heating thick specimens fast makes the specimen temperature lag. Heat thick specimens slowly
std: ASTM E1640 (assignment of the glass transition temperature by DMA)

tensile.name: Tensile testing
tensile.what: Pull a specimen to measure Young's modulus, the yield point or 0.2% proof stress, tensile strength, elongation and reduction of area. The basic strength values of a material.
tensile.how: The specimen is pulled at a constant rate while force and extension (extensometer) are recorded to give the engineering stress–strain curve.
tensile.q: Elongation depends on specimen shape and gauge length, so compare like specimens
tensile.size: Enough material to machine a standard specimen (small specimens exist)
tensile.prep: Machine a specimen of standard shape
tensile.time: Minutes to tens of minutes per specimen (days to machine specimens)
miss: Confusing the (upper) yield point with the 0.2% proof stress. Use proof stress when there is no distinct yield point
Reading the fall in engineering stress after necking as weakening of the material (the cross-section is shrinking; look at true stress)
Elongation depends on specimen shape and gauge length. Do not compare elongations of different specimen types directly
std: JIS Z 2241 (tensile testing of metallic materials)
ISO 6892-1 (tensile testing of metallic materials at room temperature)

hardness.name: Hardness testing (Vickers, Rockwell, Brinell)
hardness.what: Measure hardness from the size or depth of an indent. Quick, possible on finished parts, and used for hardness profiles through heat treatments, case-hardened layers and welds.
hardness.how: Vickers uses the diagonals of the indent of a square diamond pyramid, Brinell the diameter of a ball indent, and Rockwell the depth of a cone or ball indent.
hardness.rl: Set by the indent size (for example, about 30 µm diagonal at 0.98 N in a 200 HV steel)
hardness.vol: A small volume around the indent
hardness.q: Conversions between scales and to tensile strength are approximate and limited to tables for specific materials
hardness.size: Small pieces to parts (Rockwell or portable testers on finished parts)
hardness.ds: Leaves a small indent (portable testers measure parts as they are). Hardness profiles through layers need a cut section
hardness.prep: A polished surface for micro-Vickers; a flat surface for Rockwell and Brinell
hardness.time: Tens of seconds to minutes per indent
miss: Indents too close to each other or to an edge give wrong values because of work hardening around earlier indents or lack of support. Keep the spacings set by the standard
On thin samples or thin layers the anvil or substrate shows through. Respect the minimum thickness in the standard, and use nanoindentation for thin films
Conversions between HV, HRC and HB and to tensile strength are approximate; use only tables matching the material and heat treatment
std: JIS Z 2244-1 (Vickers hardness test)
JIS Z 2245 (Rockwell hardness test)
JIS Z 2243-1 (Brinell hardness test)
ASTM E92 (Vickers and Knoop hardness)
ASTM E110 (Rockwell and Brinell hardness by portable testers)
ASTM E140 (hardness conversion tables)
ISO 3887 (determining the depth of decarburization of steels)

nano.name: Nanoindentation
nano.what: Record force and depth continuously while indenting to nm–µm depths, and obtain hardness and Young's modulus of thin films, small phases and surface layers.
nano.how: From the load–depth curves on loading and unloading, the contact area and the initial unloading slope (contact stiffness) are found and hardness and modulus are calculated.
nano.rl: Positioning below 50 nm (indents need µm spacing)
nano.rd: Displacement noise below 0.1 nm, up to about 20 µm
nano.vol: A small volume around the indent
nano.q: Indenting shallower than 10–20% of the film thickness is the usual rule, but for a hard film on a soft substrate the substrate shows through even at 5%
nano.prep: Flat, smooth surface (roughness scatters the values)
nano.time: Minutes per indent; hours for a map
miss: Substrate properties mix into the film value. For a hard film on a soft substrate the substrate shows through even at shallow depths
Rough surfaces and films thinner than 10 nm give semi-quantitative values only
Indentation hardness (instrumented) and Vickers hardness are defined differently. Do not compare the numbers directly
std: ISO 14577-1 (instrumented indentation test for hardness and materials parameters)

charpy.name: Charpy impact testing
charpy.what: Break a notched specimen with one swing of a pendulum and compare toughness (whether it fails in a brittle way) by the absorbed energy. Tests at several temperatures reveal the ductile–brittle transition.
charpy.how: The energy used to break the specimen is found from the difference between the height the pendulum is raised to and the height it swings up to afterwards.
charpy.q: Values scatter even at one temperature, so several specimens are averaged. Values are for comparison with specifications and cannot be converted into fracture toughness
charpy.size: Enough material to machine a standard specimen
charpy.prep: Machine to standard shape, cut the notch, condition to temperature
charpy.time: Minutes per specimen (days to machine and condition specimens)
miss: Using absorbed energy as a fracture toughness for design. Results are for comparison with each other or with a specification
Comparing at one temperature only. In the transition region small temperature differences change the value greatly, so test at several temperatures and draw the curve
Also record the crystalline (brittle) versus fibrous (ductile) fraction of the fracture and the lateral expansion
std: JIS Z 2242 (Charpy impact test of metallic materials)
ISO 148-1 (Charpy pendulum impact test)
ASTM E23 (notched bar impact testing)

fatigue.name: Fatigue testing
fatigue.what: Apply cyclic loading and count cycles to failure to obtain the S–N curve and the fatigue limit (fatigue strength). Crack growth rate (da/dN) tests are another form.
fatigue.how: Several specimens at different stress amplitudes are cycled until they fail or reach a set number of cycles (run-out).
fatigue.q: Lives scatter widely (log life is close to normally distributed), so test enough specimens and treat the data statistically
fatigue.prep: Machine specimens and finish their surfaces
fatigue.time: 10⁷ cycles take about 12 days at 10 Hz; weeks to months overall
fatigue.cost: High (long use of the test machine)
miss: Deriving a design curve (mean minus two standard deviations) from few data. Small samples underestimate the standard deviation, which is unconservative
Putting run-outs (unbroken specimens) into the regression as if they had failed
Striation spacing on the fracture surface is a guide to crack advance per cycle. Read it together with SEM fractography
std: ASTM E466 (force-controlled constant-amplitude axial fatigue tests)

creep.name: Creep testing
creep.what: Hold a constant load at high temperature and record strain against time (creep curve) and time to rupture. The basis of life assessment for high-temperature components.
creep.how: A specimen in a furnace carries a constant load while its extension is logged for a long time. Rupture times are organized by temperature and stress (Larson–Miller parameter etc.).
creep.q: Some programmes aim at the stress that causes rupture in 100,000 hours (about 11 years)
creep.ds: Broken (or deformed for a long time)
creep.time: Hundreds to tens of thousands of hours
creep.cost: High (long use of furnaces and machines)
miss: Extrapolating short-term results too far. Check the assumptions of parameter methods (no change of mechanism) and state the extrapolation range
Small temperature differences change rupture life greatly. Verify temperature control and measurement
std: ASTM E139 (creep and creep-rupture tests of metallic materials)

raman.name: Raman spectroscopy
raman.what: Measure molecular and lattice vibrations from tiny wavelength shifts in scattered laser light to identify carbon forms (diamond, graphite, amorphous), oxides and polymers, and stress in semiconductors, at a 1 µm spot. No vacuum and nondestructive.
raman.how: Scattered light whose wavelength has changed by exchanging energy with molecular or lattice vibrations (Raman scattering) is dispersed and recorded.
raman.el: Sees bonds and crystal types, not elements (pure metals give no peaks; oxides and rust can be measured)
miss: Strong fluorescence swamps the much weaker Raman signal (try another excitation wavelength)
Quantification is difficult without standards
Each spectrum comes from a ~1 µm spot. Measure many spots on inhomogeneous samples

ftir.name: Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy
ftir.what: Identify polymers, organics, contamination and coatings from infrared absorption by functional groups. With ATR, simply pressing a solid onto the crystal probes roughly the top 0.1–2 µm.
ftir.how: Infrared light at the frequencies of molecular vibrations is absorbed; an interferometer and Fourier transform record all wavelengths at once.
ftir.dl: 1–10 wt% for quantifying known components; 5–20% for identifying unknowns
ftir.q: Quantification needs standards and uniform thickness
ftir.size: Particles visible by eye to small pieces
ftir.prep: None with ATR; KBr pellets or extraction are sometimes used
miss: Metals themselves cannot be measured (only contamination or films on them)
Water absorbs strongly, so dry wet samples first
Contamination films thinner than about 100 nm are hard to see (use XPS for the outermost surface)

echem.name: Electrochemical measurements (polarization curves, EIS)
echem.what: Sweep the potential in solution and measure the current to obtain corrosion potential, corrosion rate, the passive range and pitting potential. AC impedance (EIS) follows the resistance of films and coatings and how it changes.
echem.how: A potentiostat sweeps the potential in a three-electrode cell (working electrode = sample, counter and reference electrodes). Corrosion current comes from Tafel extrapolation, or from polarization resistance and Tafel slopes (Stern–Geary equation).
echem.vol: The surface in contact with the solution
echem.q: Polarization resistance is taken from the linear range around the corrosion potential (about 10 mV or less). Scan rate and solution resistance change the value
echem.size: Small pieces with a defined exposed area
echem.prep: Mask all but the measured area; polish to a consistent finish
echem.time: Tens of minutes to hours per run (including stabilization)
miss: Fast scans mix in charging current (slow scans such as 0.1 mV/s are used)
Not correcting the potential error from solution resistance (IR drop)
Not stating the reference electrode (SCE, Ag/AgCl, SHE), so results cannot be compared
Results depend on test solution and temperature. Use conditions close to service
std: JIS G 0577 (pitting potential of stainless steels)
ASTM G59 (potentiodynamic polarization resistance)
ASTM G61 (cyclic potentiodynamic polarization for localized corrosion)

archi.name: Archimedes method (density and open porosity)
archi.what: Weigh the sample dry, saturated with water and suspended in water to obtain bulk density and the fraction of pores connected to the surface (open porosity). A basic measure of how dense a sintered body is.
archi.how: The difference between saturated and suspended weights gives the sample volume, and the weight of absorbed water gives the open-pore volume.
archi.q: Pores not connected to the surface (closed pores) are not counted
archi.size: Small pieces to parts that fit the balance
archi.ds: Non-destructive (the sample is soaked in water)
archi.prep: Weigh dry, weigh saturated, weigh suspended in water
miss: Closed pores are not counted, so do not judge density from open porosity alone (use sections or X-ray CT for closed pores)
Incomplete saturation underestimates open porosity
Materials that react with or dissolve in water cannot be measured as they are
std: ISO 18754 (density and apparent porosity of fine ceramics)

ut.name: Ultrasonic testing
ut.what: Send ultrasound into a part and receive reflections from internal flaws (cracks, voids, inclusions, weld defects) to estimate their position and size. Also measures wall thickness.
ut.how: A probe sends ultrasound at about 1–25 MHz through a couplant (water, oil etc.), and the arrival time and height of echoes from flaws and the back wall are read.
ut.rl: — (higher frequency is more sensitive to small flaws)
ut.vol: The full thickness of the part
ut.q: Echo heights are compared with reference blocks to estimate flaw size
ut.size: Small pieces to large structures (on site)
ut.prep: Smooth the contact surface and apply couplant
miss: Coarse-grained materials (austenitic welds, castings) attenuate the sound and give high noise
Without calibration on reference blocks, flaw sizes are misjudged. Needs skilled operators
Without couplant the sound does not get in
std: JIS Z 2344 (general rules for pulse-echo ultrasonic testing of metals)
JIS Z 2355-1 (ultrasonic thickness measurement: method)

pt.name: Penetrant testing
pt.what: Reveal surface-breaking cracks and pinholes as colored or fluorescent indications using a penetrant and developer. Works on any non-porous material: metals, ceramics, plastics.
pt.how: The penetrant seeps into flaws; after the surface excess is removed, the developer draws it out to form an indication.
pt.q: The indication is larger than the flaw (it bleeds)
pt.size: Small pieces to large parts (on site)
pt.prep: Clean off oil, paint and dirt thoroughly and dry
pt.time: Tens of minutes (including dwell and development)
miss: Flaws that do not break the surface (internal or subsurface) are not found
Porous materials retain penetrant everywhere and cannot be tested
Insufficient pre-cleaning leaves oil or paint plugging the flaw mouths, so flaws are missed
std: JIS Z 2343-1 (penetrant testing: general principles)

mt.name: Magnetic particle testing
mt.what: Magnetize steel or another ferromagnetic material and collect magnetic particles where flux leaks out at surface and near-surface cracks.
mt.how: Flux leaks out at a flaw and the particles (fluorescent ones exist) gather there to form an indication. Sensitivity is best when the flux is perpendicular to the flaw.
mt.q: The indication length gives a guide to crack length
mt.size: Small pieces to large parts (on site)
mt.cond: Ferromagnetic materials only (steel, cast iron, Ni, Co…)
miss: It does not work on non-ferromagnetic materials (austenitic stainless steel, Al, Cu…); use penetrant or eddy current testing
Cracks parallel to the flux are hard to see. Magnetize in two directions
std: JIS Z 2320-1 (magnetic particle testing: general principles)

et.name: Eddy current testing
et.what: Induce eddy currents in a conductor with a coil to find surface and near-surface cracks, differences in material (conductivity) and plating or coating thickness, quickly and without contact. Used for 100% inspection of tubes and wire.
et.how: Flaws or material changes disturb the eddy currents and change the coil impedance. Higher frequencies see only shallower depths (skin effect).
et.rd: Penetration depends on frequency, conductivity and permeability (the standard depth of penetration is where intensity falls to 37%)
et.q: Signal size is judged against reference standards
et.size: Small pieces to large parts, tubes and wire
et.prep: Almost none (surface condition affects the signal)
miss: Only conductors can be tested
Deep flaws are not seen; penetration is set by frequency, conductivity and permeability
Flaws parallel to the coil winding or the scan direction are easily missed
Without reference standards, signal size cannot be related to flaw size
std: JIS Z 2316-1 (eddy current testing: general principles)

rt.name: Radiographic testing
rt.what: Pass X-rays or gamma rays through a weld or casting onto film or a detector to find internal porosity, lack of fusion and cracks. Leaves a permanent record.
rt.how: Voids and low-density regions let more radiation through and appear darker on the image.
rt.rl: — (as a guide, voids about 2% of the thickness are visible: about 0.5 mm in 25 mm of steel)
rt.rd: The thickness is projected (no depth information)
rt.q: Judged from density differences on the image (image quality checked with IQIs)
rt.size: Small pieces to large structures (on site)
rt.prep: Almost none (film or detector must fit behind)
rt.time: Minutes to expose; hours including processing and evaluation
miss: Thin cracks show only when the beam is parallel to the crack plane. Shoot from several directions
Radiation protection (controlled areas, qualified staff) is required
The image is a projection, so the depth of a flaw is unknown (use UT or CT)
std: JIS Z 3104 (radiographic testing of steel welds)
